holding_summary: In holding that the Emergency Rent Laws protect the widow of a deceased statutory tenant, the court reasoned by analogy that the statute already protects paying lodgers and boarders, even strangers, who reside with a tenant's household so long as the letting is merely incidental to the tenant's own dwelling occupancy; a fortiori the tenant's own widow must be protected.

quotes.text: Obviously the Legislature did not intend to exclude from the operation of the statute premises occupied as a dwelling not only by the tenant, but also by self-supporting members of the family who pay rent or board to the head of the household, and it can hardly be contended that the Legislature intended to exclude from its operation similar cases where the paying guests are not related and perhaps strangers to the tenant so long as the renting of the rooms to strangers is merely incidental to the occupation of the premises by the tenant as his dwelling.

If the protection of the Emergency Rent Laws is to be extended to lodgers and members of the household paying board or rent, with how much more force can it now be urged that such statutes should be held to extend to the widow and children of a deceased statutory tenant, in order to insure their continued occupancy of their home now that its head has gone.

notes: Core holding concerns widow's succession to statutory tenancy; the favorable lodger/boarder doctrine is adopted reasoning quoted approvingly from May v. Dermont, not the case's own facts.

holding_summary: The plaintiff, who was in the business of renting furnished apartments for profit, leased a furnished apartment to the defendant for one year; the defendant sublet it to a physician who held over after the lease expired. The court held the defendant liable for two months' rent as a holdover tenant, ruling he was not a statutory tenant entitled to Emergency Rent Law protection because he was a landlord who had sublet the furnished apartment to a third party for profit rather than occupying it as his own dwelling.

quotes.text: The plaintiff, Helena Marsh Goodwin, was engaged in the business of renting furnished apartments for profit.
Defendant Was not a statutory tenant, but a landlord who leased the apartment to a third party for profit.

Where a tenant occupies rooms in a dwelling leased by him and leases rooms by weekly or monthly letting, “ it is not a house used for dwelling purposes, but is a house used for business ” (Nystad & Krassner, Inc., v. Zerbe, 210 App. Div. 217), and he is not “ a statutory tenant ” as to the.rooms or floors sublet.

notes: Marked mixed: the court treats commercial furnished-apartment letting/subletting as ordinary lawful business (favorable to the practice), but excludes it from dwelling-protective rent-law statutes because it is profit-driven rather than owner-occupied (adverse to statutory protection).

notes: duration_of_occupancy left unclear because the building housed both long-term permanent residents and short-term transient guests concurrently; a tax exemption case rather than a licensing/police-power case, but bears on lodging-house characterization.
